summary: Describes how COPS should be used to provide policy services in RSVP environments. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: This is the instruction sheet for using the manager-checking system when handing out network reservations.

subtitle: How a router hands RSVP reservation decisions to a policy server using the COPS protocol.

tldr.problem: RSVP routers need to check reservation requests against network policy, but the policy lives on a separate server. COPS is a general query and response protocol and needs RSVP-specific rules.
tldr.mechanism: RSVP is COPS client-type 1. The router (PEP) sends the RSVP objects to the policy server (PDP) with a context for incoming, resource-allocation or outgoing processing, and the PDP answers with Install or Remove plus optional extra data.
tldr.outcome: It gives a precise usage profile for outsourcing RSVP policy decisions, including flows, caching, commit reports, error reporting and worked examples.

today: RFC 2749 is a Proposed Standard from January 2000, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on RFC 2748 for COPS and RFC 2205 for RSVP.

sections.title: COPS Meets RSVP
sections.content:
The Common Open Policy Service (COPS) protocol is a query and response protocol that exchanges policy information between a network policy server and a set of clients. It was developed in the RSVP Admission Policy Working Group, mainly to provide policy-based admission control over requests for network resources.

This RFC assumes you already know the RAP framework (RFC 2753) and basic COPS (RFC 2748). It gives usage directives for the case where RSVP clients, called PEPs (policy enforcement points), outsource policy control decisions to policy servers called PDPs (policy decision points). Because COPS is designed to be generic, the RSVP directives are mostly about applicability, interoperability, usage guidelines and examples.
sections.eli5: A router is like a ticket clerk who has to phone the manager before giving out a special pass. This sheet explains how that phone call should go for network reservations.

sections.title: RSVP Values for COPS Objects
sections.content:
The common header's client-type is 1 for RSVP. The Context object says which of three moments the request is about:

  • Incoming-Message: the PEP received an RSVP message. If the PDP rejects it, RSVP treats it as if it never arrived.
  • Resource-Allocation: the PEP is about to commit local resources. This applies to Resv messages only and covers the merge of all reservations for the flow on one interface.
  • Outgoing-Message: the PEP is about to forward a message. The PDP may allow or deny it and supply outgoing policy data.

The M-Type reuses the RSVP msg type values. Supported types are Path, Resv, PathErr and ResvErr. PathTear, ResvTear and Resv Confirm are not supported.

The Client Specific Information object carries every object from the RSVP message. For Resource-Allocation it must contain the SESSION and STYLE objects with the merged FLOWSPEC, the FILTERSPEC list and the SCOPE object where relevant. If the PDP finds a required RSVP object missing, it should return the error 'Mandatory client-specific info missing'. If an optional object it needs is missing, it should return a negative decision.
sections.eli5: The router tells the manager which step it is at: a letter just arrived, a seat is about to be reserved, or a letter is about to be sent on. The manager answers for that step.

sections.title: How the PDP Answers: Decisions
sections.content:
Only two decision commands apply to RSVP: Install (accept, allow or admit a message or allocation) and Remove (deny, reject or remove it). The only decision flag is Trigger Error, which tells RSVP to schedule a PathErr or ResvErr.

Stateless Policy Data adds policy elements, such as a preemption priority, to the decision. The PEP can only add them, not override the decision, and a PEP may legitimately ignore ones it does not support, so the PDP must be prepared for that.

Replacement Data swaps RSVP objects in the message. A replacement object replaces all instances of the same C-Num, and an empty one (length 4) removes them. RSVP clients are only required to allow replacement of POLICY_DATA, ERROR_SPEC and FLOWSPEC. If no Replacement Data appears, the signaled objects are processed as if the PDP was not there.
sections.eli5: The manager can say 'yes' or 'no', add a sticker with a priority number, or swap parts of the form for different ones.

sections.title: Flows, Caching and Commit Reports
sections.content:
Policy control is done per RSVP flow, the atomic unit of a reservation. Reservation style matters: senders treated as one flow under a WF reservation count as separate flows under FF. Several FF flows may be packed in one Resv message, and the PEP must unpack them and issue a separate request for each.

After a reservation passes both policy control and capacity admission control, the PEP sends a report of type Commit, which signals when billing should begin. If a PDP-approved reservation fails admission for lack of resources, the PEP issues a no-commit report and returns to the previous state, or sends a delete request (DRQ) if there was none. PathTear and ResvTear are not under policy control.

Because COPS is stateful, the PEP can cache a decision and apply it to Path and Resv refreshes, updating the PDP when the message changes. If the connection to the PDP is lost, cached state may be kept for the RSVP timeout period for previously admitted flows only. After that the PEP is expected to purge it, and must reject flows or use its local policy decision point (LPDP) if it has one. A reconnected PDP may issue a state sync request (SSQ), and the PEP must then reissue requests for its current state.

Multiple context flags may be combined in one request only in two cases: unicast FF (incoming, allocation and outgoing) and multicast with a single Resv received on the interface (incoming and allocation). For errors, the PEP queries the PDP before sending PathErr or ResvErr, and the PDP returns the ERROR_SPEC in a Replacement Data decision.
sections.eli5: The router remembers the manager's last answer so it need not phone again for every repeat. It only phones again when something changes, and it tells the manager once the reservation is truly in place.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
In the unicast example, a router with interfaces if1 and if2 sits between receiver R1 and sender S1. A Path message from S1 triggers a request for the incoming and outgoing contexts, and the PDP installs it. A Resv from R1 triggers one request for all three contexts. The PDP's decision is split into one section per context, including a stateless priority of 7 and a replacement POLICY-DATA object. The PEP sends a Commit report.

Later the PDP changes its decision to priority 3. Because that is too low, the PEP preempts the flow with a DRQ and the reason code Preempted. When S1 stops sending Path messages, the PEP sends another DRQ with the reason Timeout.

The multicast example has two senders, three receivers and a shared media interface. When a second reservation with a higher RSpec arrives on the same interface, the PEP can no longer combine contexts and issues incoming and allocation requests separately. The outgoing Resv then carries the merged reservations.
sections.eli5: The examples show full phone calls between the router and the manager, including the manager changing its mind so the router has to cancel a reservation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC relies on COPS for its own signaling and security and points to the security section of RFC 2748. Security for RSVP messages comes from inter-router MD5 authentication and a chain-of-trust model.

A likely deployment has PEPs only at the network edge, with policy-ignorant nodes in the core. MD5 trust is then established between non-neighboring boundary PEPs, through internal signing of the Policy Data object, which is left unmodified as it passes through the core nodes.
sections.eli5: The routers check each other's signatures, and the phone line to the manager is protected by the COPS rules.

items.label: Positive response
items.desc: Accept, allow or admit an RSVP message or local resource allocation.

items.label: Negative response
items.desc: Deny, reject or remove an RSVP message or local resource allocation.
